summary:
Consensual same-sex relations have been legal across Tajikistan since May 1998, and consensual sex between women was never criminalised. The age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Decriminalisation has not produced protection: Tajikistan has no non-discrimination protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the country's first anti-discrimination law, adopted in July 2022, dropped sexual orientation and gender identity as protected grounds and retained only sex. International monitors assess that 2022 law as only partially aligned with UN standards, and a 2020 ECOM legislative analysis built from questionnaires completed by local partners records legal barriers and gaps affecting gay men, men who have sex with men and trans people, including cases where the written law protects but practice does not.

Authorities maintain a register of LGBTIQ people introduced by police in 2016 and described by Outright International as a 2017 government registry of "proven" LGBT persons. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025, covering 2024, reports that police lure LGBT people into fake meetings in order to register them in a database, harvest their social-media contacts and extort money, with more than ten such cases recorded in Sughd province. Sughd is one prefecture-level example of a national pattern, not an isolated locality: the IPHR report 'Rights for All?' (February 2024) documents police raids in 2022 and 2023 that brought forced HIV testing and arbitrary criminal charges, alongside documented ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by police. ECOM recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people in 2024, involving arbitrary arrest, blackmail and extortion by police.

Forced and sham marriages are used against LGBT people, with police inaction recorded in the same review. The 2022 anti-discrimination law is also cited as failing to address discrimination in practice.

Trans visitors face a distinct set of obstacles. Gender-affirming medical services are not available in Tajikistan, so trans people must travel abroad to medically transition, and most doctors have no expertise in the treatments trans people need. Legal gender recognition is blocked in practice: Tajik law permits reassignment on some documents, but medical institutions issue no official documents for that purpose. A diagnosis of transsexualism is required, surgery is required for transgender women but not men, and evaluation is carried out by commissions of three psychiatrists on an unregulated, case-by-case basis in which activists report that bribes are often necessary. Only three to six people are recorded as having successfully changed their legal gender.

Same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to married heterosexual couples, and no relationship-recognition framework exists.

The wider environment compounds the legal picture. Public expression of support for LGBT people is effectively suppressed and public attitudes have been described as entirely negative, in a condition of hypervisibility in which homophobic and transphobic remarks from politicians form part of everyday politics. The Supreme Mufti, Saidmukarram Abdulkodirzoda, has called same-sex relations a disaster, condemned countries legalising same-sex marriage, and spoken against human-rights activists and anti-discrimination laws. People who disclose their orientation become targets of physical and psychological abuse, including from police, a pattern reported well before the 2016 register was created.
tangentialFactors:
Tajikistan's LGBT situation sits inside a broader repressive state context. HRW's World Report 2017 records that the human-rights situation deteriorated sharply in 2016, with opposition leadership sentenced, human-rights lawyers imprisoned and a predetermined referendum extending presidential rule. The register of LGBTIQ people introduced by police in the same year emerged from that environment.

Prison and detention reporting in HRW's World Report 2025 concerns opposition figures, including Group 24 and Islamic Revival Party detainees, and deportees. The chapter records no placement or conditions of trans detainees, so detention risk for trans visitors cannot be assessed from that source.

ECOM's 2024 study on trans people's access to medical services, including HIV prevention and treatment and hormone replacement therapy, covers the wider Eastern Europe and Central Asia region and includes guidance for trans migrants; a Tajikistan country coordinator contributed to it. The regional framing means its recommendations travel with a trans visitor crossing borders rather than describing Tajik-only service conditions.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ groups in Tajikistan operate anonymously, one focused solely on trans issues and one on general LGBTQ issues. Activists have no access to the Ministry of Health or other state authorities, which makes state-level advocacy impossible. A trans-focused non-governmental organisation has drafted a hormone-replacement-therapy protocol now used to educate endocrinologists.

Residents report disrespectful treatment by medical staff, and some Tajik psychologists and doctors offer pseudoscientific methods that present homosexuality as an addiction comparable to alcoholism or drug addiction. Access to the police register and to the extortion and blackmail documented against LGBT people in 2024 is a domestic enforcement pattern, with more than ten entrapment cases recorded in Sughd province alone.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether trans detainees are held, and under what conditions, is unresolved: HRW's World Report 2025 records nothing on the subject for Tajikistan, and no other source in the inventory addresses it.

No findings were located on LGBTQ minors, education-sector policies or school environments, so school and age-related exposure is not sourced either way.

The counts of successful legal-gender changes (three to six people), the description of public attitudes as "entirely negative," the characterisation of hypervisibility in everyday politics and the account of bribe-dependent psychiatric commissions derive from Wikipedia's country coverage, a secondary compilation; the primary documents behind those figures were not reviewed here.

ECOM's 2024 trans-medicine study is cited at the level of its regional scope and its inclusion of Tajikistan-specific material; the Tajikistan country section's individual findings are not enumerated in the available inventory.
